heading: Combining small livestock
body: Combining small livestock makes chickens, ducks and bees working members of the farm.
Learn how animals can control pests, build soil fertility, support pollination, and return value to the soil.
Use the system you already have: food, manure, flowers, grazing and moving with care across all the land.

heading: Why this matters
body: Small livestock can do work beyond producing meat, eggs or honey.
Chickens eat some pests and weed seed. Their manure can become compost.
Ducks scratch less than chickens, but may still damage crops.
Bees and other pollinating insects help many crops. Each animal still needs suitable food, water, shelter and care.

heading: Learning outcomes
body: At the end of this lesson, you will understand how chickens, ducks, bees and guinea fowl fit into a working system.
You will know when chickens help the bed, and when their scratching can do damage.
You will understand pollination, where to put a beehive, and how livestock move nutrients around the farm.

heading: Watch: chickens look for food after harvest
body: Watch chickens looking for food on the ground among dry crop remains.
Chickens may eat some pests and weed seed. They still need properly nutritious food, clean water and shelter.
Keep them away from seedlings and food that is ready to be harvested.

heading: Chickens turn scratching into useful work
body: Chickens can help on an empty bed after harvest.
They scratch among crop remains and eat some pests and weed seed.
Their manure and bedding can be made into compost and returned to the soil.
Finding their own food does not take the place of properly nutritious food, clean water, shelter and care every day.

heading: Use chickens at the right time
body: Use chickens on an empty bed after harvest.
Keep them away from seedlings and crops harvested for eating.
Fresh manure can have germs. Ask an agricultural mentor to tell you how to deal with manure safely before the next crop.
Move the birds before they damage the soil.

heading: Ducks suit the lower level that is set up
body: Ducks eat slugs and snails without the strong scratching of chickens.
They may suit the lower level of an established food forest.
They may eat or trample crops and make wet soil muddy. Watch the birds and move them when necessary.
Give clean water and suitable food; finding their own food alone may not be enough.

heading: Rotate the chicken tractor around the site
body: A chicken tractor is a moving coop, without a floor.
Move it before the soil is without plants, muddy, or heavily covered with manure.
The right time depends on the birds, the soil and the weather. Let the soil recover between visits.
No single number of chickens guarantees that there will be enough fertility across the whole site.

heading: Watch: a bee moves between two flowers
body: Watch one bee moving from one flower to another.
Bees can carry pollen as they visit flowers.

heading: Bees help pollination of many crops
body: Honeybees and other insects carry pollen between flowers.
This helps many fruit and vegetable crops, including avocado. Crops and different varieties differ in what they need for pollination.
A hive does not guarantee a better harvest everywhere. Weather, water, plant health and other pollinating insects are important too.

heading: South Africa's native honeybees
body: South Africa has two small kinds of native honeybee.
The Cape honeybee is found in the Western Cape and in some other parts of the Eastern Cape. The African honeybee is native to central Africa and most of southern Africa.

These broad natural areas are not a guide for moving bees. The Department's control measures set a dividing line that controls the movement of bees. Check the current rules before moving bees or hives.

heading: Place the hive carefully
body: Learn from an experienced local beekeeper before getting a hive.
Keep hives away from busy roads, homes and places where children play.
Morning sun can help, but a safe place matters first.
Plan the way people and animals will walk around the place.

heading: Strong bee colonies need care and flowers
body: Give flowering plants in all seasons of the year and avoid exposing bees to pesticides.
Active bees are not proof that the farm has no chemicals or diseases.

Registration is needed for activities described by the national honeybee control measures. This includes keeping controlled hives for bee products, raising queens, commercial pollination, and removing, destroying or moving bee colonies. Ask the Department if you are not sure whether your activity is covered.
If a colony swarms repeatedly, ask a trained beekeeper to inspect it. Crowding is one of the possible reasons, not a diagnosis of the problem.

heading: Nutrients that move on the farm
body: Some nutrients move out of the crops to the animals. Bought feed also brings nutrients onto the farm. Some nutrients may return to the growing area through compost made from manure. Food and other products remove nutrients.

heading: Some nutrients come back; others go in and out
body: Animals can return some nutrients through compost made from manure. Fresh manure can have dangerous germs. Rot the manure completely before you use it near food crops.
Chickens eat suitable farm produce and pests.
Bought feed brings nutrients onto the farm. Food that is sold or taken home and other products remove nutrients. Keep a record of the bought feed and the food sold or taken home.
Food scraps alone may not meet the animals' needs.

heading: Guinea fowl find their own food, but health checks are still important
body: Guinea fowl look for insects and may eat ticks.
Do not trust them to protect people or livestock from ticks or from diseases carried by ticks.
Keep checking the animals and follow the local animal health plan.
Birds that find their own food are part of the farm, they do not take the place of health care.

heading: Ask three questions about each animal
body: For each animal, ask what it can eat here.
Ask what useful things it produces.
Then ask what else it needs. Combine water, suitable food, shelter, fencing and care every day.
Some needs may require bought things. Plan for them before bringing animals onto the land.

heading: Grazing and goat worm control
body: Chickens that follow goats are not a proven way to take the place of goat worm control.
Grazing management can help, but goats still need health checks.
Work with a vet or animal health mentor on a parasite plan for your herd.
Do not stop treatment because chickens visited the grazing camp.

heading: Fieldwork: draw where the resources go
body: Walk around your small farm and choose a place where livestock can support another part of the system.
Write down the food, leftover food, insects, leftover produce, manure or flowering resources that are already there.
Then mark what each animal can produce, and what it will need from the farm.
Draw one useful relationship between the livestock and another part of your farm. Show what goes in and what goes out.

heading: Field action: use one relationship
body: Choose one safe action from this lesson.
Plan how chickens could use an empty bed after harvest, ask a beekeeper about a safe place for a hive, or check your animals' daily needs.
Write down the food, water, shelter and care that this action requires.
Start with the resources and help you can reliably provide.
